1.problem: In the interior of a square \(ABCD\) we construct the equilateral triangles \(ABK, BCL, CDM, DAN.\) Prove that the midpoints of the four segments \(KL, LM, MN, NK\) and the midpoints of the eight segments \(AK, BK, BL, CL, CM, DM, DN, AN\) are the 12 vertices of a regular dodecagon.
1.solutions:
Just use complex numbers, with \(a = 1\), \(b = i\), \(c = - 1\) and \(d = - i\). With some calculations, we have \(k = \frac {\sqrt {3} - 1}{2}( - 1 - i)\), \(l = \frac {\sqrt {3} - 1}{2}(1 - i)\), \(m = \frac {\sqrt {3} - 1}{2}(1 + i)\) and \(n = \frac {\sqrt {3} - 1}{2}( - 1 + i)\). Now it’s an easy job to calculate the twelve midpoints and to find out they are all of the form \(\frac {\sqrt {3} - 1}{2}e^{\frac {k\pi}{6}i}\), with \(k\in\mathbb{N}: 0\le k\le 11\), and the result follows.

The above solution was posted and copyrighted by Joao Pedro Santos.

Solution 2

Synthetic solution:

Clearly the four first midpoints form a square with midpoint \(O\) where \(O\) is the midpoint of \(ABCD\). Hence it suffices to check that the other eight points have the same distance from \(O\) and that the angles at \(O\) are correct.

By symmetry, it will then suffice to check that \(\triangle OEF\) is equilateral where \(E\) is the midpoint of \(KL\), and \(F\) is the midpoint of \(AK\). Being midlines in triangles \(\triangle AKL\) and \(\triangle AKC\), we see that \(EF = \frac{1}{2} AL\) and \(OF = \frac{1}{2} KC\). On the other hand, in the square \(KLMN\) we clearly have \(EO = \frac{1}{2} KL\). But by construction, the triangles \(\triangle ABL, \triangle LBK, \triangle KBC\) are all congruent whence \(AL = LK = KC\), and hence \(EF = EO = OF\) as desired.

(This solution was posted by Tintarn on the discussion page mentioned below. This solution (just like the one above) would benefit from the addition of some details, but it is nevertheless a good solution.)

Solution 3

In this solution we use analytic (coordinate) geometry. Let us take the origin to be at \(A\), and the axes to be along \(AB, AD\). We can assume the square \(ABCD\) has side \(2\), so the four vertices are \(A = (0, 0), B = (2, 0), C = (2, 2), D = (0, 2).\)

Let \(e_k, k = 1, \dots, 12\) be the mid points specified in the problem. (Note that it seems that the mid points have some additional properties, for example \(e_3\) seems to be on \(BL\), \(e_5\) seems to be on \(DM\), etc. We are not interested in this now, so we will not investigate these properties.)

The plan is to compute the coordinates of \(K, L, M, N\), then compute the coordinates of \(e_k, k = 1, \dots, 12\). This will enable us to compute the lengths of the segments \(e_1e_2, e_2e_3, \dots, e_{12}e_1\), the slopes of these segments, and the angles between adjacent segments. Noticing that the lengths and angles are respectively equal, will have solved the problem. Note that we don’t have to compute all of them. Because of various symmetries, it is enough to compute some of them.

Specifically, we will compute the coordinates of \(e_3, e_4, e_5, e_6\), the lengths of \(e_5e_6\) and \(e_4e_5\), the slopes of \(e_5e_6, e_4e_5, e_3e_4\), which will let us determine the angles at \(e_5\) and \(e_4\).

An easy computation yields that the points \(K, L, M, N\) have coordinates \(K = (1, \sqrt{3}), L = (2 - \sqrt{3}, 1), M = (1, 2 - \sqrt{3}), N = (\sqrt{3}, 1)\).

Then we have

\(e_3 = \left( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right), e_4 = \left( \frac{3 - \sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{3 - \sqrt{3}}{2} \right), e_5 = \left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \right), e_6 = \left( \frac{4 - \sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \right).\)

A trivial computation shows that the squares of the lengths of \(e_4e_5, e_5e_6\) are both \(7 - 4\sqrt{3}\).

Now remember that if we have two points \(P = (p_x, p_y), Q = (q_x, q_y)\) then

slope of \(PQ = \tan(\)of the angle between \(PQ\) and the positive direction of the \(x\)-axis\() = \frac{p_y - q_y}{p_x - q_x}\).

In our case, the slope of \(e_5e_6\) is clearly 0. A trivial computation shows that the slope of \(e_5e_4\) is \(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \tan 150^{\circ}\).

A similar computation shows that the slope of \(e_4e_5\) is \(-\sqrt{3} = \tan 120^{\circ}\).

We conclude that the angles at \(e_5, e_4\) are both \(150^{\circ}\), as expected (since the angles of a regular dodecagon are supposed to be \(150^{\circ}\)).

2.problem: In a finite sequence of real numbers the sum of any seven successive terms is negative and the sum of any eleven successive terms is positive. Determine the maximum number of terms in the sequence.
2.solutions:
Let \(x_1,x_2,\ldots\) be the given sequence and let \(s_n=x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_n\). The conditions from the hypothesis can be now written as \(s_{n+7}<s_n\) and \(s_{n+11}>s_n\) for all \(n\ge 1\). We then have: \(0<s_{11}<s_4<s_{15}<s_8<s_1<s_{12}<s_5<s_{16}<s_9<s_2<s_{13}<s_6<s_{17}<s_{10}<s_3<s_{14}<s_7<0,\) a contradiction. Therefore, the sequence cannot have \(17\) terms. In order to show that \(16\) is the answer, just take 16 real numbers satisfying \(s_{10}<s_3<s_{14}<s_7<0<s_{11}<s_4<s_{15}<s_8<s_1<s_{12}<s_5<s_{16}<s_9<s_2<s_{13}<s_6\). We have \(x_1=s_1\) and \(x_n=s_n-s_{n-1}\) for \(n\ge 2\). Thus we found all sequences with the given properties.

The above solution was posted and copyrighted by enescu. The original thread for this problem can be found here: https://aops.com/community/p369641

3.problem: Let \(n\) be a given number greater than 2. We consider the set \(V_n\) of all the integers of the form \(1 + kn\) with \(k = 1, 2, \ldots\) A number \(m\) from \(V_n\) is called indecomposable in \(V_n\) if there are not two numbers \(p\) and \(q\) from \(V_n\) so that \(m = pq.\) Prove that there exist a number \(r \in V_n\) that can be expressed as the product of elements indecomposable in \(V_n\) in more than one way. (Expressions which differ only in order of the elements of \(V_n\) will be considered the same.)
3.solutions:
Lemma: there are \(\infty\) many prime numbers \(p ot\equiv 1 \mod n\).

Proof:

Assume that there are only finitely many of them and let their product be \(k\). Then all prime factors of \(nk - 1\) must be \(\equiv 1 \mod n\) since this number is coprime with \(k\). But that would mean that \(- 1 \equiv nk - 1 \equiv 1 \mod n\) which is impossible for \(n > 2\).

Now we can tackle the problem: There are only finetely many residue classes \(\mod n\), thus we can find two primes \(p,q\) with \(p \equiv q ot\equiv 1 \mod n\) and coprime with \(n\). Let \(s\) be the smallest positive integer with \(p^s \equiv 1 \mod n\), then the same property holds for \(q\) too. Now we have that \(p^s, q^s, pq^{s - 1} , p^{s - 1}q \equiv 1 \mod n\) are all indecomposable since all their nontrivial divisors are \( ot\equiv 1 \mod n\). But the product \(p^sq^s = (pq^{s - 1})(p^{s - 1}q)\) gives a number that is represented in two ways.

The above solution was posted and copyrighted by ZetaX.

Remark and Solution 2

The lemma is incorrect. A simple example: k=5, n=3, 2 is a prime factor of nk-1=14 but 2≡2 (not 1) mod n.

Following is my approach. We build \(r=abcd\), \(ab \equiv cd \equiv ac \equiv bd \equiv 1\) mod \(n\), \(ab,cd,ac,bd\) are indecomposable, \(a eq d, b eq c\). Then \(r=ab \cdot cd=ac \cdot bd\) satisfies the requirement. Let \(a,b,c,d\) all be written in the form of \(kn-1\), so that their pairwise products \(\equiv 1\) mod \(n\). We set the values of elements as small as possible to maximize the chance of being indecomposable. So we set \(a=b=n-1\), \(c=d=2n-1\).

\(ab=(n-1)^2<(n+1)(2n+1)\), therefore indecomposable;

\(ac,bd=(n-1)(2n-1)<(n+1)(2n+1)\), therefore indecomposable;

\(cd=(2n-1)^2\), if it’s decomposable, its factors must include \(n+1\), because the only element in \(V_n\) smaller than \(2n-1\) is \(n+1\). Then \((n+1) | (4n^2-4n+1)=4n(n+1)-8n+1\), \((n+1) | (8n-1)=8(n+1)-9\), therefore \((n+1) | 9\), \(n+1=1,3,9\), since \(n \ge 3, n=8\), meaning if \(n eq 8, (2n-1)^2\) is indecomposable;

If \(n eq 8\), set \(a=b=n-1, c=d=2n-1\), \(r=ab \cdot cd=ac \cdot bd\), \(ab=(n-2)n+1\), \(ac=bd=(2n-3)n+1\), \(cd=(4n-4)n+1\), all conforming to the form of \(kn+1\); As aforementioned, \((n-1)^2, (n-1)(2n-1), (2n-1)^2\) are now all indecomposable, and obviously \((n-1)^2 eq (n-1)(2n-1)\), valid;

If \(n=8\), we can take \(a=b=n-1=7, c=d=3n-1=23\), \(r=49 \cdot 529=161 \cdot 161=25921\), the first few elements are: \(n+1=9, 2n+1=17, 3n+1=25\), and the only prime factors of \(49, 161, 529\) are \(7\) and \(2\)3, therefore they are indecomposable, valid.

Proof completed.

Remarks (added by pf02, March 2026)

\(\mathbf{1}\): The remark in the first sentence of Solution 2 (saying that "The lemma is incorrect...", referring to the Lemma in the first Solution) is wrong. There is nothing wrong with the Lemma, it is correct.

Also, I made some editing of Solution 2 (for readability), and I corrected one typo.

Solution 2 is badly incomplete (in addition to being so sloppily written); it relies too heavily on hand-waving. The shortcomings are in the fact that in order to prove that \((n - 1)^2\) and \((n - 1)(2n - 1)\) are indecomposable, it is not enough to compare them to \((n + 1)(2n + 1)\) (or, it is not obvious why this would be enough). Also, for showing that \((2n - 1)^2\) is indecomposable, it is not enough to only consider the case when \(n + 1\) is one of its factors. These shortcomings can be fixed by a diligent reader, and I will not complete this proof.

\(\mathbf{2}\): Following this remark, I transcribe a solution from the discussion page https://aops.com/community/p397316 by Taha1381.

\(\mathbf{3}\): After Solution 3, I will add a remark which simplifies the solution.

Solution 3

By Dirichlet’s Theorem (see also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet\%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions) there are infinity many primes congruent to \(-1\) modulo \(n\). Take two of them, \(p eq q\). Then \((pq)(pq) = (p^2)(q^2) = p^2q^2 \in V_n\). Obviously \(pq, p^2, q^2\) are indecomposable, so we are done.

This is a rewriting of the solution by Taha1381 from the discussion page (original thread) mentioned below.

Remark about Solution 3

We don’t need the full force of Dirichlet’s theorem. All we need is to show that there are infinitely many primes congruent to \(-1\) modulo \(n\). (Dirichlet’s theorem tells us much more: there is an infinite arithmetic progression of such primes). This can be shown with a proof similar to the proof of Euclid’s Theorem about the infiniteness of primes:

Assume that there would be only finitely many primes \(p\) such that \(p \equiv -1 \mod n\). Let \(p_1, \dots, p_r\) be all these primes. Let \(k = p_1 \dots p_r\). Now let \(q\) be a prime factor of \(kn - 1 = n p_1 \dots p_r - 1\). So, \(n p_1 \dots p_r - 1 = qa\) for some number \(a\). On the one hand, \(q eq p_j\) by construction. On the other hand, \(q \equiv -1 \mod n\) by construction. This is a contradiction, because \(p_1, \dots, p_r\) were all the primes \(\equiv -1 \mod n\).

4.problem: Let \(a,b,A,B\) be given reals. We consider the function defined by \[f(x) = 1 - a \cdot \cos(x) - b \cdot \sin(x) - A \cdot \cos(2x) - B \cdot \sin(2x).\] Prove that if for any real number \(x\) we have \(f(x) \geq 0\) then \(a^2 + b^2 \leq 2\) and \(A^2 + B^2 \leq 1.\)
4.solutions:
\(f(x) = 1-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sin (x+\arctan\frac{a}{b}) - \sqrt{A^2+B^2}\sin (2x+\arctan\frac{A}{B}) \geq 0\). \(f(x+\pi) = 1+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sin (x+\arctan\frac{a}{b}) - \sqrt{A^2+B^2}\sin (2x+\arctan\frac{A}{B}) \geq 0\)

Therefore, \(\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\sin (2x+\arctan\frac{A}{B}) \leq 1\). Since this identity is true for any real \(x\), let the sine term be one, \(\longrightarrow A^2+B^2 \leq 1\).

To get cancellation on the rightmost terms, note \(\sin (x+\pi/2) = \cos x, \sin (x-\pi/2) = -\cos x\).

\(f(x+\pi/4) = 1-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sin (x+\pi/4+\arctan\frac{a}{b}) - \sqrt{A^2+B^2}\cos2x+\arctan\frac{A}{B}) \geq 0\). \(f(x-\pi/4) = 1-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sin (x-\pi/4+\arctan\frac{a}{b}) + \sqrt{A^2+B^2}\cos2x+\arctan\frac{A}{B}) \geq 0\).

Let \(x+\arctan\frac{a}{b} = y\). Then \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}(\sin (y+\pi/4) + \sin (y-\pi/4)) \leq 2\)

\(\sqrt{a^2+b^2} \leq \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}(\sin y)}\).

Since it’s valid for all real \(y\) let \(\sin y = 1\), and we are done.

The above solution was posted and copyrighted by aznlord1337.

Remarks (added by pf02, March 2026)

If we want to be rigorous, the proof above is incorrect. The problem is that it uses the formula

\(a \cos x + b \sin x = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \sin (x + \arctan \frac{a}{b})\)

This should be

\(a \cos x + b \sin x = \mathbf{sgn}(b) \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \sin (x + \arctan \frac{a}{b})\)

and it is valid when \(b \ne 0\).

However, the idea of the proof is good, and it is not difficult to make it rigorous.

The original thread for this problem can be found here: https://aops.com/community/p1351208

5.problem: Let \(a,b\) be positive integers. When \(a^2 + b^2\) is divided by \(a + b\), the quotient is \(q\) and the remainder is \(r\). Find all pairs \((a, b)\) such that \(q^2 + r = 1977\).
5.solutions:
Using \(r=1977-q^2\), we have \(a^2+b^2=(a+b)q+1977-q^2\), or \(q^2-(a+b)q+a^2+b^2-1977=0\), which implies \(\Delta=7908+2ab-2(a^2+b^2)\ge 0\). Using AM-GM inequality and the fact a,b>0, we have 3(a+b)̂2<=7908+8ab<=7098+8(a+b)̂2/4, it follows \(a+b\le 88\). If \(q\le 43\), then \(r=1977-q^2\ge 128\), contradicting \(r<a+b\le 88\). But \(q\le 44\) from \(q^2+r=1977\), thus \(q=44\). It follows \(r=41\), and we get \(a^2+b^2=44(a+b)+41\Leftrightarrow (a-22)^2+(b-22)^2=1009\in \mathbb{P}\). By Jacobi’s two squares theorem, we infer that \(15^2+28^2=1009\) is the only representation of \(1009\) as a sum of squares. This forces \(\boxed{(a,b)=(37,50) , (7, 50)}\), and permutations. \(\blacksquare\)

The above solution was posted and copyrighted by cobbler.

Solution 2

We start like in the first solution. Replacing \(r\) by \(1977 - q^2\), we get the equation in \(q\): \(q^2 - (a + b) q + (a^2 + b^2 - 1977) = 0\). Since this equation has real solutions, we have \((a + b)^2 - 4(a^2 + b^2 - 1977) = -3a^2 + 2ab + 7908 - 3b^2 \ge 0\).

The expression \(-3a^2 + 2ab + 7908 - 3b^2\) has some non-negative values, so the equation in \(a\): \(-3a^2 + 2ab + 7908 - 3b^2 = 0\) has real roots. (Equivalently, we could use the fact that the vertex of the parabola \(y = -3a^2 + 2ab + 7908 - 3b^2\) has positive \(y\).) It follows that \(b^2 + 3(7908 - 3b^2) = 4(5931 - 2b^2) \ge 0\). This implies \(b \le 54\). Similarly \(a \le 54\).

Now \(1977 = q^2 + r < q^2 + a + b \le q^2 + 108\) from which we get \(q > \sqrt{1977 - 108}\), so \(q \ge 44\). On the other hand, \(q^2 \le 1977\), so \(q \le 44\). It follows that \(q = 44\). This implies \(r = 41\).

We now have to solve \(a^2 + b^2 = 44(a + b) + 41\) where \(a, b\) are positive integers. As an equation in \(a\) this is \(a^2 - 44a + (b^2 - 44b - 41) = 0\). We have \(a = 22 \pm \sqrt{484 - b^2 + 44b + 41}\). The expression under the square root has to be a square, say \(525 - b^2 + 44b = c^2\) for some \(c\), or \((b - 22)^2 + c^2 = 1009\).

We now want to find all the possible pairs of squares which add to \(1009\). There are 32 squares from \(0^2 = 0\) to \(31^2 = 961\) to be considered \((32^2 = 1024 > 1009).\) In looking for pairs which add up to \(1009\), we can discard the squares \(\le 36\). We discard \(49, 64\) as well, since they can not be used in a pair of squares which adds to \(1009\). Note that the last digit of squares is one of \(0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9\). So we can discard squares whose last digit is \(1\) or \(6\), and only consider pairs of squares whose last digits are \(4\) and \(5\), or \(0\) and \(9\). The remaining squares we have to consider are \(100, 144, 169, 225, 324, 289, 400, 484, 529, 625, 729, 784, 900\).

Let us look at the sequences \(144, 225, 324, 484, 625, 784\) and \(100, 169, 289, 400, 529, 729, 900\). From each sequence choose pairs of numbers which add up to \(1009\). Obviously, the only pair is \(225 = 15^2\) and \(784 = 28^2\). Thus, we can have \(b - 22 = \pm 15\) or \(b - 22 = \pm 28\). This gives the possible values for \(b\) to be \(b = 7, 37, 50\). From \(a = 22 \pm \sqrt{484 - b^2 + 44b + 41}\) we get the corresponding values for \(a\) (keep only the positive ones). This yields the values for \((a, b)\) to be \((7, 50), (37, 50), (50, 7), (50, 37)\).

6.problem:
Let \(f(n)\) be a function \(f: \mathbb{N}^{+}\to\mathbb{N}^{+}\), where \(\mathbb{N}^{+}\) is the set of positive integers. Prove that if

\[f(n+1) > f(f(n))\]

for each positive integer \(n\), then \(f(n)=n\).
6.solutions:
We will prove this via induction. First we will prove there is a \(t\) such that \(f(t)=1\) and then that \(t=1\) is the only such solution.

Define the sequence \(a_n\) with \(a_0>1\) for \(a_0\in \mathbb{N}\) and \(a_k=f(a_{k-1}-1)\). By the given inequality we have that \(f(a_n)>f(a_{n+1})\), this can be used to form a inequality chain of decreasing positive integers: \[f(a_0)>f(a_1)>f(a_2)>...\]

By Infinite Descent, this sequence must terminate, and the only way it can terminate is if we input something into \(f\) that is outside of its range. This can only happen if \(a_n=1\) since the range and domain of \(f\) are the positive integers. Since \(a_0\neq 1\), there is a integer \(t\) (\(a_{n-1}-1\)) such that \(f(t)=1\).

Now if \(t\neq 1\), then \(f(t)=1>f(f(t-1))\), which is impossible since \(f(f(t-1))\ge 1\) by the range of \(f\), so we have \(t=1\) is the only time when \(f(t)=1\).

Now for the inductive step.

Assume that \(f(n)=n\) for all \(n<k\) and these are the only times these values occur. We will prove that \(f(k)=k\) and that this is the only time this value occurs. Define the sequence \(a_n\) similarly, except that \(a_0>k\), by the reasoning above, there is a \(a_m\) such that \(f(a_m)=1\), by the inductive assumption, this means that \(a_m=f(a_{m-1}-1)=1\), we can repeat the inductive assumption to get that \(a_{m-k+1}=k\). This implies that \(f(a_{m-k}-1)=k\). Thus, there is a \(t\) such that \(f(t)=k\).

Now for that \(t\), we have \(k>f(f(t-1))\), which means that \(k+1>t\) by the inductive assumption which implies \(t=k\) since we must have \(t>k-1\), otherwise \(f(t)<k\). So \(t=k\) is the only time when \(f(t)=k\)

So the inductive step is complete. Therefore, by induction \(f(n)=n\) for all positive integers \(n\).

Solution 2

First, we will prove that \(f\) is strictly increasing.

To prove this, we will prove by induction on \(k\) that

\(f(1) < f(2) < \dots < f(k) \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (a)\)

and

\(f(n) > f(k)\) for \(n \ge k + 1 \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (b)\)

First, prove the case \(k = 1\). There is nothing to prove for \((a)\). For \((b)\), let \(m = \min\{f(n), n \ge 1\}\). We will show that if \(p\) is such that \(f(p) = m\) then \(p = 1\).

Suppose \(p > 1\). Then we can take \(f(p - 1)\). The number \(f(p - 1)\) is in \(\mathbb{N}^+\), so we can take \(f(f(p - 1))\). We have \(m \le f(f(p - 1))\) because of the definition of \(m\), \(f(f(p - 1)) < f(p)\) by hypothesis, and \(f(p) = m\) because of the choice of \(p\). Putting it all together, we have \(m \le f(f(p - 1)) < f(p) = m\), which implies \(m < m\). This contradiction tells us that the assumption \(p > 1\) is false, i.e. \(p = 1\).

Let us now assume \((a), (b)\) true for \(k\), and prove them for \(k + 1\).

Let \(M = \{n, n \ge k + 1\}\), and let \(m = \min\{f(n), n \in M\}\) (in other words, \(m = \min\{f(n), n \ge k + 1\}\)). Choose \(p \in M\) such that \(f(p) = m\). We will show that \(p = k + 1\).

\((a)\) says \(f(1) < f(2) < \dots < f(k)\); we deduce that \(f(k) \ge k\). (Indeed, if we have a strictly increasing sequence of \(k\) numbers, the last one has to be \(\ge k\).)

Note that because of \((b)\), we have \(m > f(k)\). (Indeed, \(m = f(p)\) for a \(p \ge k + 1\).)

Now suppose \(p > k + 1\). Then \(p - 1 \in M\), so if we take \(f(p - 1)\), we have \(f(p - 1) \ge m\).

Putting the last three inequalities together, we have \(f(p - 1) \ge m > f(k) \ge k\), in other words, \(f(p - 1) > k\). Thus \(f(p - 1) \in M\) (i.e. \(f(p - 1) \ge k + 1\)).

It follows that \(m \le f(f(p - 1))\). Combine with \(f(f(p - 1)) < f(p)\) (from the hypothesis), and \(f(p) = m\) (from the choice of \(p\)) to get \(m \le f(f(p - 1)) < f(p) = m\), or \(m < m\). This contradiction shows that our assumption \(p > k + 1\) was wrong, so \(p = k + 1\).

Both \((a)\) and \((b)\) follow from this.

Now we will show that \(f(n) = n\). From the fact that \(f\) is strictly increasing, we have \(f(n) \ge n\) (we used this argument above). We want to show that \(f(n) = n\). Let \(k\) be such that \(f(n) = n + k\), and suppose \(k \ge 1\).

If \(k = 1\), then \(f(n + 1) = f(f(n)) < f(n + 1)\) (from \(n + 1 = f(n)\) and the hypothesis), which is a contradiction.

If \(k > 1\), we have

\(f(n) < f(n + 1) < \dots < f(n + k - 1)\)

because \(f\) is strictly increasing. Applying \(f\) once more, we have

\(f(f(n)) < f(f(n + 1)) < \dots < f(f((n + k - 1))\)

Combine with \(n + k = f(n)\) and \(f(f(n + k - 1)) < f(n + k)\) (by hypothesis) and get

\(f(n + k) = f(f(n)) < f(f(n + 1)) < \dots < f(f(n + k - 1)) < f(n + k)\)

which implies \(f(n + k) < f(n + k)\). This contradiction shows that the assumption \(k \ge 1\) can not be true, so \(k = 0\), i.e. \(f(n) = n\).
